correctness.limits: No extension to smaller orders, arbitrary forests, skew forcing or positive-semidefinite forcing; finite tests do not establish general truth.
correctness.rationale: Proof shows that four or more initially white vertices cannot force twice: two tree vertices cannot share two neighbors. For exactly two whites, failed forcing occurs precisely for sibling leaves. For three whites, a valid initial center is equivalent to selecting two of its neighbors that are not both leaves plus an outside nonneighbor; at most two centers can be valid and exactly the unoriented five-vertex paths cause double-counts. Star complement is a clique plus an isolate. The O(n) identity follows by neighbor-sum expansion. A standard-library verifier independently tested 3,134,704 initial white sets over 20,110 trees, including all labeled trees at orders 5–7; the proof handles all n>=5.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The complete polynomial strictly refines the extremal degree information. In particular the nonisomorphic spiders with arm sequences (1,1,3) and (1,2,2) have the same vertex-degree multiset and zero-forcing number of the complement, but differing coefficients (8,14) and (11,15). Thus the scalar theorem, degree sequence alone, and original-tree comparison results do not imply this distribution without a new argument.

value.rationale: Counts every ordinary zero-forcing set for the natural infinite class of tree complements, extending a known scalar minimum-degree theorem to a full invariant. Supplies an O(n) arithmetic evaluation and a genuinely structural P5 correction to avoid nontrivial witness overlap. It distinguishes two six-vertex trees with identical degree sequences and the same zero-forcing number, demonstrating more information than an extremal or degree-only parameter. It is not a finite instance or arbitrary parameter slice.
